messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Thomas Njoku, a 59-year-old African American professor at a local university, has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic event that occurred nearly six months ago. The trauma was not personal to him but involved his late wife, who tragically drowned in a sudden flood during one of their weekend trips to the beach. Since then, Dr. Njoku's life has been irrevocably altered by his recurring memories and intense reactions. The event itself was overwhelming: they were enjoying a peaceful day at the beach when an unexpected flash flood struck. Dr. Njoku vividly recalls seeing water rising swiftly around them, and despite his frantic efforts to help, he watched in horror as his wife struggled against the surging waters before she was swept away. The sound of her panicked screams and the sight of her desperate attempts to hold on have haunted him ever since. For Dr. Njoku, any visual cues reminiscent of water or flooding trigger a cascade of intense distress. At work, he finds himself particularly affected by the science department's aquarium or even the smell of chlorine from the campus swimming pool, both of which instantly transport him back to that fateful day at the beach. His body reacts before his mind can process what is happening; his heart races, and he feels an overwhelming sense of fear and helplessness, much like it did when he saw the water rise around his wife. These triggers not only evoke strong negative emotions but also reinforce a pervasive sense of threat. Dr. Njoku finds himself constantly on edge, unable to relax even in safe environments. He has become hyper-vigilant, always scanning for any signs that might remind him of the traumatic event. This heightened state of alertness means that he is easily startled by sudden movements or unexpected noises, particularly those associated with water. His reactions have become self-reinforcing: each time Dr. Njoku encounters a trigger, his body responds immediately with fear and anxiety, which then reinforces his belief that danger lurks around every corner. This cycle has led him to avoid many situations that once brought him joy, such as teaching hydrology courses or attending social events near bodies of water. The weight of these experiences has taken its toll on Dr. Njoku’s daily life. He finds it increasingly difficult to focus during lectures and often skips departmental outings to the beach for conferences. His colleagues have noticed a change in his demeanor, describing him as distant and preoccupied. Despite his professional success, he feels isolated, unable to share the burden of these memories with others. What frightens Dr. Njoku most is the fear that he will never be able to escape this cycle of triggers and threats. He worries about how much longer he can continue teaching without succumbing to these overwhelming feelings. His frustration has finally pushed him to seek help, hoping to find a way to reclaim his life from the shadows of trauma. Dr. Njoku is seeking therapy not only to manage his symptoms but also to regain a sense of control and peace in his daily routine. He hopes that with support, he can learn to navigate his triggers without the paralyzing fear that currently dominates his thoughts and actions.
